---
title: "One-sample t inference"
execute:
  enabled: true

The paired Hillenbrand contrast yields one duration difference per adult woman. One-sample t inference represents uncertainty in the mean of those speaker-level differences while estimating their scale from the same observations.

We first derive the t reference from a standardized sample mean, then compute the paired vowel contrast from the observed speakers, and finally interpret the interval and test under the assumptions attached to those speaker-level differences.

## From a standardized mean to a t reference

For independent differences $D_1,\ldots,D_n$ from a normal population,

$$
\frac{\overline D-\mu_D}{\sigma_D/\sqrt n}\sim\mathcal N(0,1)
$$

and

$$
\frac{(n-1)S_D^2}{\sigma_D^2}\sim\chi^2_{n-1}.
$$

Under normal independent sampling, the sample mean $\overline D$ and sample variance $S_D^2$ are independent. The variance has $n-1$ degrees of freedom because the deviations $D_i-\overline D$ sum to zero; after estimating the mean, only $n-1$ deviations can vary freely. Write

$$
Z=\frac{\overline D-\mu_D}{\sigma_D/\sqrt n}
\quad\text{and}\quad
U=\frac{(n-1)S_D^2}{\sigma_D^2}.
$$

Then $Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$, $U\sim\chi^2_{n-1}$, and $Z$ is independent of $U$. The [Student-t construction](../random-variables-and-distributions/student-t-distribution.qmd#construction) gives

$$
\frac{Z}{\sqrt{U/(n-1)}}
=
\frac{\overline D-\mu_D}{S_D/\sqrt n}
\sim t_{n-1}.
$$

Replacing $\sigma_D$ by $S_D$ gives

$$
T=\frac{\overline D-\mu_D}{S_D/\sqrt n}\sim t_{n-1}.
$$

The corresponding interval is

$$
\overline D\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,n-1}\frac{S_D}{\sqrt n}.
$$

This interval comes from inverting the central reference event

$$
\mathbb{P}
\left(
-t_{1-\alpha/2,n-1}
\leq
\frac{\overline D-\mu_D}{S_D/\sqrt n}
\leq
t_{1-\alpha/2,n-1}
\right)
=1-\alpha
$$

for $\mu_D$. Thus the test and interval are two views of the same standardized sampling result.

## Computing the paired contrast

```{r}
#| label: hillenbrand-one-sample-t
library(ggplot2)

vowels <- read.csv(
  "data/hillenbrand/vowels-complete.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
long <- subset(vowels, speaker_type == "woman" & vowel %in% c("I", "i"),
               select = c(speaker_id, vowel, duration_ms))
paired <- reshape(long, idvar = "speaker_id", timevar = "vowel", direction = "wide")
names(paired)[names(paired) == "duration_ms.I"] <- "hid_ms"
names(paired)[names(paired) == "duration_ms.i"] <- "heed_ms"
d <- paired$hid_ms - paired$heed_ms

n <- length(d)
d_bar <- mean(d)
s_d <- sd(d)
se_d <- s_d / sqrt(n)
df <- n - 1L
t_observed <- d_bar / se_d
critical <- qt(0.975, df)
interval <- d_bar + c(-1, 1) * critical * se_d
p_value <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_observed), df) # dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation

check <- t.test(d, mu = 0)
stopifnot(
  abs(unname(check$statistic) - t_observed) < 1e-12,
  max(abs(unname(check$conf.int) - interval)) < 1e-10
)

data.frame(mean_ms = d_bar, sd_ms = s_d, se_ms = se_d,
           t = t_observed, df = df, p_value = p_value,
           lower_ms = interval[1], upper_ms = interval[2])
```

The interval is [`r sprintf("%.3f", interval[1])`, `r sprintf("%.3f", interval[2])`] ms. The two-sided tail area is `r format(p_value, digits = 4, scientific = TRUE)`.

```{r}
#| label: plot-hillenbrand-t-reference
#| fig-cap: "t reference density for the within-speaker duration statistic. The vertical lines mark the observed two-sided cutoffs."
t_grid <- data.frame(t = seq(-12, 12, length.out = 1000L))
t_grid$density <- dt(t_grid$t, df)

ggplot(t_grid, aes(t, density)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey25", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-abs(t_observed), abs(t_observed)),
             color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = paste0("t statistic (", df, " df)"), y = "Null reference density") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The normality assumption concerns the speaker differences, not the two vowel distributions separately. And the screened cohort does not make the speakers a probability sample of all American English speakers. The procedure quantifies uncertainty under the stated model; recruitment determines the scope of the conclusion.

The code maps directly to the derivation: `s_d / sqrt(n)` estimates the standard error, `qt(0.975, df)` supplies the central $t$ cutoff, `d_bar + c(-1, 1) * critical * se_d` inverts the reference event, and `t.test()` checks the hand calculation.

## Recap and forward link

1. Normal independent sampling makes $\overline D$ independent of $S_D^2$.
2. Estimating one mean leaves $n-1$ degrees of freedom in the centered deviations.
3. Replacing $\sigma_D$ by $S_D$ produces a Student-t, rather than normal, pivot.
4. The assumptions concern speaker-level differences, and recruitment limits the population claim.

The [paired-observation page](paired-observations.qmd#pairing-changes-the-variance) turns to aligned semantic graphs, where translation structure determines the pairs.

## Check your understanding

1. Why does estimating $\sigma_D$ change the reference family?
2. Which values determine the degrees of freedom?
3. Why should diagnostics focus on $D_s$?
4. What does the interval say about the direction and magnitude of the cohort contrast?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Replacing the unknown $\sigma_D$ with the random estimate $S_D$ adds scale uncertainty, yielding a $t$ rather than a normal reference distribution. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The number of independent speaker differences and the number of estimated mean parameters determine $n-1=47$ degrees of freedom. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The one-sample model is applied to the within-speaker differences, so its distributional assumptions concern $D_s$, not the two vowel margins separately. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The 95% interval is $[-77.868,-53.007]$ ms: in this cohort, /I/ in *hid* is shorter than /i/ in *heed* by about 53 to 78 ms on average. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
